Risk of Bias Assessment The risk of bias assessment is presented in Figures 2 , 3 . Most studies did not clearly show how to generate random sequences, nor did they clearly state whether association obfuscation was performed. In terms of masking method, most of the studies have insufficient information to permit judgment of “Low risk” or “High risk”. We assessed three trials having high risk of bias for different reasons. One of the trials did not report all the pre-specified primary outcome indicators ( 30 ). The random allocation method in one of the studies was incorrect (The patients were randomized according to the birth date) ( 41 ). Since Nagata reported that participants were all female college students from the same university in the trial ( 33 ), it was marked as “high risk” in other bias. Figure 2 Risk of bias. Figure 3 Summary of risk of bias. Overall Analyses Allergic Rhinitis Symptoms Score AR symptoms score included rhinoconjunctivitis total symptom score (RTSS) and total nasal symptom scores (TNSS). RTSS includes five individual AR symptoms (nasal congestion, sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal pruritus, and eye itching) noted from 0 (no symptom) to 3 (severe symptom). TNSS were expressed as the sum of the scores for the four symptoms (nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, nasal itching, and sneezing) noted from 0 (no symptom) to 3 (severe symptom). Seven trials reported pre- and post-treatment data of AR symptoms score available for meta-analysis. Compared with placebo, probiotics significantly improved AR symptoms score (SMD, −0.29, 95% CI [−0.44, −0.13]). There was high heterogeneity in the result ( p = 0.0003, I 2 = 89%) ( Figure 4 ). Sensitivity analysis indicates that the result is robust ( Supplementary Material 13 ). Due to the significantly statistical heterogeneity encountered in the analysis, several subgroup analyses were conducted separately according to the classification of AR, combination of drugs, and intervention of treatment group. Figure 4 Forest plot for allergic rhinitis symptoms score. With regard to classification of AR, probiotics can significantly relieve symptoms in patients with SAR (SMD −0.56, 95% CI [−0.87, −0.25]; p = 0.0003, I 2 = 0%), and there was significant benefit that probiotics supplementation relieved PAR symptoms score (SMD,−0.19, 95% CI [−0.37, −0.01]; p = 0.03, I 2 = 94%) ( Supplementary Material 1 ). Subgroup analysis according to the combination of drugs again found some evidence of a protective effect of probiotics (monotherapy) in relieving AR symptoms compared with placebo (SMD, −0.73, 95% CI [−1.05, −0.42]; p < 0.00001, I 2 = 93%). Compared with antihistamines, probiotics combined with antihistamines (combination therapy) have no significant relief of AR symptoms (SMD, −0.15, 95% CI [−0.32, 0.03]; p = 0.10, I 2 = 61%) ( Supplementary Material 2 ). The results of subgroup analysis showed that probiotics (single) compared with placebo cannot significantly relieve symptoms (SMD, −0.49, 95% CI [−1.05, 0.07], p = 0.09). Similarly, probiotics combined with antihistamines compared with antihistamines have no significant relief of AR symptoms (SMD, −0.15, 95% CI [−0.32, 0.03], p = 0.10, I 2 = 61%). Probiotics (mixed) compared with placebo have significant relief of AR symptoms (SMD, −0.85, 95% CI [−1.23, −0.46], p < 0.0001, I 2 = 97%) ( Supplementary Material 3 ) ( Table 2 ). Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire Score Seven trials reported pre- and post-treatment data of Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ) scores available for meta-analysis. The results combined with the fixed-effect model showed a significant decrease in RQLQ scores in the probiotic group compared with the control group (−0.64, 95% CI [−0.79, −0.49], p < 0.00001, I 2 = 97%) ( Figure 5 ). Sensitivity analysis indicates that the result is stable ( Supplementary Material 13 ). Figure 5 Forest plot for Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire Score. Subgroup analysis according to the classification of AR found some evidence of a significant decrease in RQLQ scores for SAR in the probiotic group compared with the control group (SMD, −0.32, 95% CI [−0.49, −0.15], p = 0.0002, I 2 = 96%), and a greater beneficial effect in PAR (SMD, −2.10, 95% CI [-2.45, −1.74], p < 0.00001, I 2 = 97%) ( Supplementary Material 4 ). Subgroup analysis according to the combination of drugs again found some evidence of a protective effect of probiotics (monotherapy) in relieving AR symptoms compared with placebo (SMD, −1.74, 95% CI [−2.03, −1.46]; p < 0.00001, I 2 = 97%). Compared with antihistamines, probiotics combined with antihistamines (combination therapy) have a significant relief of AR symptoms (SMD, −0.21, 95% CI [−0.39, −0.03]; p = 0.02, I 2 = 0%) ( Supplementary Material 5 ). The results of subgroup analysis showed that probiotics (single) comparing with placebo can significantly relieve symptoms (SMD, -3.81,95% CI [-4.29, -3.32], p<0.00001, I2=0%). Similarly, probiotics combined with antihistamines (combination therapy) compared with antihistamines showed significant improvement in RQLQ scores (SMD, −0.21, 95% CI [−0.39, −0.03], p = 0.02, I 2 = 0%) ( Supplementary Material 6 ) ( Table 2 ). Adverse Events Of the twenty-eight studies included, seventeen RCTs mentioned that no obvious adverse events were found during the research, while seven RCTs did not mention whether any adverse events occurred. Four RCTs have reported adverse events including diarrhea, abdominal pain, flatulence, and fever episodes. One study reported that loose stools and diarrhea were observed in the active and placebo groups, which had no significant differences in adverse events between the two groups (chi-square test, p < 0.4) ( 17 ). Another study showed that subjects with these adverse drug reactions (diarrhea, abdominal pain, and flatulence) recovered within a few days. In this study, it was found that one subject’s adverse reaction was almost certainly related to the drug ( 15 ). One study reported slight abdominal pain in probiotic groups and all of the adverse events were spontaneously alleviated without drug treatment ( 41 ). One study revealed that abdominal symptoms (abdominal symptoms, diarrhea, and fever episodes) were reported in 56.5% versus 64.2% of children in intervention and control groups, respectively ( p = 0.282) ( 26 ). Discussion In this study, the clinical evidence of probiotics in the treatment of AR was systemically collated and analyzed so as to provide a better guidance for clinical practice. Our results showed that probiotics supplementation for patients with AR can ameliorate AR symptoms and improve the quality of life. Probiotics supplementation can correct the Th1/Th2 balance. There was no significant change in overall or antigen-specific IgE levels between probiotic-treated and placebo-treated subjects. The results of this study have significant heterogeneity, and the source of heterogeneity was explored by subgroup analysis. The results of subgroup analysis showed that probiotics can significantly relieve AR symptoms in patients with SAR. Subgroup analysis according to combination of drugs again found some evidence of a protective effect of probiotics (monotherapy) in relieving AR symptoms compared with placebo. Compared with antihistamines, probiotics combined with antihistamines (combination therapy) have no significant relief of AR symptoms. Subgroup analyses of these outcomes failed to find out the source of heterogeneity. The different doses, durations, and strains of probiotics may be the sources of heterogeneity. With regard to RQLQ score, the results of subgroup analysis according to combination of drugs showed that probiotics (single probiotic strain) compared with placebo can significantly improve the quality of life. Similarly, probiotics combined with antihistamines (combination therapy) compared with antihistamines showed a significant decrease in RQLQ scores, which means an improvement in the quality of life. As we all know, helper T cells play a key role in the adaptive immune response. Human T helper cells can be divided into two main subtypes, Th1 and Th2. The significant trend of immune response to Th2 lineage may lead to allergic diseases. Immunoglobin E (IgE)-mediated allergic inflammation is the main pathophysiological mechanism of AR and drives T helper 2 (Th2) cell polarized immune reactions ( 45 ). The balance Th1/Th2 is associated with AR. Th2 induces the activation of B cells and IgE class switching, which leads to B-cell differentiation into plasma cells that produce allergen-specific IgE. IgE enters the circulation and binds through its Cϵ3 domain to the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcϵRI) on the surface of mast cells and basophils ( 46 ). Activated mast cells and basophils release inflammatory mediators (e.g., histamine and leukotrienes) that cause symptoms such as nasal itching, sneezing, and runny nose. At the same time, these inflammatory mediators lead to a predominance of Th2 immune responses, further exacerbating inflammation. Therefore, the predominance of Th2 and its related cytokines correlates with the severity of AR. The Th1/Th2 ratio can reflect the effect of improving allergy symptoms by drugs to a certain degree. Our meta-analysis demonstrated that probiotics supplementation can correct the Th1/Th2 balance, which indicates that probiotic supplementation can ameliorate AR by regulating the balance of Th1/Th2. However, only four of the included studies reported the Th1/Th2 ratio. The purpose of most systematic reviews or meta-analyses is to explore the preventive effect of probiotic supplementation on allergic diseases ( 47 – 50 ). There are less systematic reviews or meta-analyses to explore the therapeutic effect of probiotics on AR. A systematic review and meta-analysis of probiotics in the treatment of AR published in 2015 has shown that probiotics may be beneficial in improving symptoms and quality of life in patients with AR ( 51 ). One meta-analysis showed that probiotics have beneficial effects in the treatment of AR, especially with SAR and LP-33 strains ( 52 ). However, previous systematic reviews failed to explore the causes of heterogeneity as much as possible. Compared with previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses, our meta-analysis conducted subgroup analysis according to types of AR (PAR/SAR) and treatment plan (single probiotic strain/mixed probiotic strains/probiotics combined with antihistamines; monotherapy/combined). We found that a single probiotic strain (LP-33) can significantly improve the quality of life of patients with AR from the meta-analysis of three studies. Two studies used mixed probiotic strains. One study demonstrated that a Bifidobacteria mixture ( B. longum BB536, B. infantis M-63, and B. breve M-16 V) was able to significantly improve AR symptoms and quality of life in children with pollen-induced AR and intermittent asthma ( 39 ). Another study showed that probiotic NVP-1703 (a mixture of B. longum and L. plantarum ) relieves AR symptoms by prompting Treg cells to release IL-10 ( 42 ). However, there was a high heterogeneity from meta-analysis of two studies, which may be related to the use of different probiotics. The different strains of probiotics, doses, and durations may be the sources of heterogeneity. To date, no serious adverse events have been observed for probiotic treatment; thus, it appears to be safe. To sum up, probiotic supplement seems to be effective in ameliorating AR symptoms and improving the quality of life, but there is high heterogeneity in some results after subgroup analysis, and clinicians should be cautious when recommending probiotics in treating AR. There are some limitations in this meta-analysis. First, the sample size of some included RCTs was small. Second, airborne pollen concentrations are associated with symptom severity and recovery in patients with SAR. The pollen concentrations varied due to different regions in different trials. This is a source of clinical heterogeneity. Conclusion This study found that in spite of the positive results of some outcomes, there is weak evidence that probiotics have a potential benefit in the treatment of AR. More RCTs using specific probiotic strains and consistent outcome measures are also needed in the future to investigate efficacy and safety. documents.title: Prevalence of IVIG resistance in Kawasaki disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Kawasaki Disease (KD) is an acute vasculitis primarily affecting children, with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) being the standard treatment and leading to increased risk of coronary artery abnormalities.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to evaluate the prevalence of IVIG resistance in KD and identify potential predictors and outcomes associated with this resistance.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Medline, Embase, and other relevant databases was conducted to identify studies reporting IVIG resistance in KD patients. Data on prevalence rates, patient demographics, and associated factors were extracted and analyzed.
RESULTS: The analysis included 26 studies with a total of 46,461 patients. The overall prevalence of IVIG resistance was found to be 14% (95% CI: 12%-16%), and The prevalence among males and females was 9% (95% CI; 7% to 10%) and 4% (95% CI; 3.7% to 4.3%), respectively.
CONCLUSION: IVIG resistance remains a significant challenge in the management of KD. Identifying patients at higher risk for IVIG resistance and developing alternative treatment strategies are crucial for improving outcomes in this population.
documents.conclusions: IVIG resistance remains a significant challenge in the management of KD. Identifying patients at higher risk for IVIG resistance and developing alternative treatment strategies are crucial for improving outcomes in this population.

Introduction Kawasaki Disease (KD) is an acute systemic vasculitis primarily affecting children under the age of five. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children, with coronary artery lesions (CALs) being the most common and life-threatening complication. If left untreated, CALs can lead to severe outcomes such as coronary artery dilatation, aneurysm formation, lumen stenosis, occlusion, and potentially fatal myocardial infarction ( 1 ). KD triggers the release of various inflammatory factors, resulting in a cascade amplification effect. Although KD is a self-limited inflammatory process, it can become life-threatening depending on the extent of cardiac involvement. Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, including fever, exanthema, conjunctivitis, changes in extremities, erythema of oral mucosa and lips, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Early recognition and treatment are crucial to lower the risk of cardiac complications, the etiology of KD remains unknown, though clinical, laboratory, and epidemiological features suggest an infectious origin or trigger. Immune system activation is a notable feature of KD, with elevated concentrations of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines being studied for their potential to improve future anti-inflammatory therapies ( 2 ). The standard treatment for KD involves high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) at 2 g/kg combined with aspirin, reducing the incidence of CALs from 20%–25% to 2%–4%. However, initial IVIG treatment fails in 7.5%–26.8% of KD patients, who continue to experience inflammatory reactions and remain at risk for CALs. Severe complications such as Kawasaki disease shock syndrome or macrophage activation syndrome can occur, posing significant threats to patient survival. Thus, in-depth analysis of factors influencing IVIG insensitivity, early prediction, and timely intervention are critical to reducing cardiac damage in IVIG-resistant KD ( 1 ). The American Heart Association (AHA) recommends early administration of IVIG to significantly reduce CAL incidence. Yet, up to 20% of KD patients exhibit IVIG resistance, strongly associated with CAL occurrence. Recent literature has focused on identifying predictors for IVIG resistance, aiming to implement additional therapeutic measures to reduce CAL incidence through early diagnosis. Research indicates various predictors, including male sex, high C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, decreased platelet counts, and elevated neutrophil ratios ( 3 ). Therefore, early identification of IVIG resistance in KD patients is vital for initiating intensive treatments such as corticosteroids, potentially benefiting these patients by reducing the risk of severe cardiac complications ( 4 ). This systematic review and meta-analysis seek to determine the prevalence of IVIG resistance in KD, assess the associated risk factors, and provide insights into the potential for early prediction and intervention. Understanding these elements is vital for optimizing treatment strategies and improving the prognosis for children affected by this complex disease. Method This systematic review and meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Search strategy A comprehensive search was conducted in the following electronic databases: PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, and ResearchRabbit from January 2008 to October 31, 2024. The search terms (Mesh) included (“Kawasaki Disease” AND “IVIG resistance”) AND (prevalence OR incidence). Additional relevant articles were obtained by searching the reference lists of the articles. The search was restricted to articles published in English. Inclusion criteria (PIOS) Population: Children diagnosed with Kawasaki disease. Intervention: Initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). Outcomes: Studies reporting the prevalence of IVIG resistance. Study Design: Cohort studies published in peer-reviewed journals. Exclusion criteria Studies were excluded from the review if they were non-original research (e.g., case reports), lacked sufficient data on IVIG resistance prevalence, involved non-cohort designs, included adult populations or mixed-age groups without separate pediatric data, used treatments other than standard-dose IVIG, were not published in English, or represented duplicate data from the same patient population. Data extraction A standardized data extraction form was developed to systematically collect relevant information from each included study. Extracted data included study characteristics such as first author, publication year, sample size, participant demographics (including age), Kawasaki disease type, laboratory parameters, and reported prevalence of IVIG resistance. Statistical analysis The meta-analysis was conducted using STATA Ver. 17 and the Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed using risk ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and continuous outcomes were analyzed using standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% CI. The random or fixed effect models were used to pool the data. The Q test and I 2 index were used to assess the heterogeneity of the studies. If the I 2 value was greater than 50%, the heterogeneity was considered substantial, and the sources of heterogeneity were explored ( 5 ). The random or fixed effect models were used to pool the data. A funnel plot was used to assess the publication bias. Meta-regression and the Eger test were used to explore the significance of publication bias ( 6 ). Results 141 related studies were found by searching in the databases, 32 studies in PubMed, 73 in Google Scholar, 24 studies in Cochrane, and 12 studies in Web of Sciences. 21 studies were found by checking the references, after removing 30 duplicate studies, 132 articles were screened and reviewed. Out of 132 studies, 98 studies were excluded based on non-relevant titles or abstracts, 8 studies were excluded for the following reasons: No original research, insufficient data, and no relevant outcomes. A total of 26 articles met our inclusion criteria and were finally included in this meta-analysis ( Figure 1 ). Figure 1 The PRISMA flow diagram includes studies. Flowchart of a systematic review process. Identification: 141 records found (PubMed: 32, Google Scholar: 73, Cochrane Library: 24, ISI: 12) plus 21 from reference checks. Screening: 132 records after duplicates; 98 excluded. Eligibility: 34 full-text articles assessed, 8 excluded for non-control group or review article. Included: 26 studies in qualitative and quantitative synthesis. Characteristics of included studies In 26 studies, the sample size was 46,461 people. While most studies included both complete and incomplete KD, a few explicitly reported data on atypical KD forms, which appear to be associated with a similar or potentially higher risk of IVIG resistance ( 4 , 12 ). Outcome Prevalence rates The meta-analysis conducted on the prevalence of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) resistance in patients with Kawasaki Disease (KD) yielded important findings. The overall prevalence of IVIG resistance was found to be approximately 14%, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 12% to 16% ( Figure 2 ). This suggests that roughly one in seven KD patients may experience resistance to IVIG treatment. When examining the data by sex, it was observed that males had a prevalence rate of 9% (95% CI: 7% to 10%), as shown in Figure 3 , while females exhibited a lower prevalence rate of 4% (95% CI: 4% to 5%) in Figure 4 . Figure 2 Forest plot of prevalence IVIG resistance in KD disease. Forest plot showing prevalence estimates from various studies with corresponding confidence intervals and weights. A red dashed line marks the summary estimate along the x-axis, labeled \"prevalence.\" The diamond at the bottom indicates the overall effect size (ES=0.14, confidence interval 0.12 to 0.16) with high heterogeneity (I2=94.17%). Individual study names and ES values are listed alongside percentages representing their weights. Figure 3 Forest plot of prevalence in males in the IVIG resistance group. Forest plot displaying the prevalence of a condition in males across multiple studies. Each study is represented by a square and horizontal line indicating the effect size and confidence interval. Weights of studies are shown as percentages. The overall pooled effect is marked by a diamond at the bottom, with an I-squared value of 87.67%, indicating heterogeneity. The x-axis measures prevalence. Figure 4 Forest plot of prevalence in females in the IVIG resistance group. Forest plot showing prevalence estimates in females from multiple studies. The x-axis displays prevalence values ranging from negative 0.2 to 0.6. Each horizontal line represents a study with a square marking the estimate and a horizontal bar indicating the 95% confidence interval. The diamond at the bottom indicates the overall summary estimate with its confidence interval. Each study’s weight and confidence interval are listed on the right. The plot reveals variability among studies, with a combined prevalence of 0.04 and significant heterogeneity, denoted by an I-squared value of 79.56%. In terms of geographical variability, the study by Yang et al. reported the lowest prevalence of IVIG resistance, at only 6% (95% CI: 5% to 5%), suggesting that the occurrence of resistance may vary across different populations and clinical settings. In contrast, the study by Fury et al. showed a much higher rate of IVIG resistance, reaching over 40%. This marked difference highlights the influence of regional factors and the need for further investigation into the underlying causes of such disparities. Further research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms behind IVIG resistance in KD and how best to tailor treatments to individual patients based on their risk profiles. Overall, this meta-analysis underscores the complex nature of IVIG resistance in KD and calls for continued investigation into its prevalence, risk factors, and potential interventions. Risk Factors and Predictors Across studies, predictors included: High CRP and neutrophil ratio Low albumin and platelet count Elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin Use of predictive scores (e.g., Egami, Kobayashi) with varied geographic accuracy. Publication bias To check publication bias and small study, an effect funnel plot was used it demonstrated that the standard error of the majority of studies was low so the precision of included studies was high. bubble plot helps summarize the data in a way that highlights the relationships between multiple variables, the distribution of those relationships, and potential areas for deeper analysis. The left plot is a bubble plot with effect size (ES) on the vertical axis and year on the horizontal. It shows data points with varying sizes and a dashed trend line from 2010 to 2025. To explore source of heterogeneity and effect of year of publication on effect size multivariate meta-regression was applied, the results of meta regression showed that there were not significant association between year of publication and effects size ( Table 2 ). Population group Covariates Coefficient Std. err t P In total year −0.0011287 0.0029123 −0.39 0.702 In male year −0.001471 0.0023117 −0.64 0.531 In female year −0.0003867 0.0023117 −0.17 0.867 Discussion The findings of this systematic review and meta-analysis provide a comprehensive understanding of the prevalence of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) resistance in Kawasaki Disease (KD), a critical challenge in managing this pediatric vasculitis. Our analysis indicates that a significant proportion of KD patients do not respond to initial IVIG treatment, with prevalence rates ranging from 7.5% to 26.8% across various studies. This variability underscores the complexity of IVIG resistance and the need for tailored approaches in clinical practice. The high prevalence of IVIG resistance observed in KD patients has significant implications for clinical management. As CALs are the most severe complication associated with KD, timely and effective treatment is crucial to prevent long-term cardiac sequelae. Our findings align with previous studies that highlight the importance of early diagnosis and intervention to mitigate the risk of CALs ( 29 , 30 ). Furthermore, understanding the factors contributing to IVIG resistance can guide the development of predictive models and personalized treatment strategies. Recent research has identified several predictors of IVIG resistance, including male gender, elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, decreased platelet counts, and higher neutrophil ratios ( 31 ). These predictors can help clinicians identify patients at higher risk of resistance and consider alternative or adjunctive therapies, such as corticosteroids, in conjunction with IVIG ( 32 ). Some studies also differentiated between complete, incomplete, and atypical KD, all of which are associated with IVIG resistance ( 4 , 12 ). Several validated scoring systems have been developed to predict IVIG resistance in KD patients, including the Egami, Kobayashi, and Sano scores. These scores incorporate clinical and laboratory variables such as age, ALT levels, CRP, and neutrophil counts to stratify patients by risk. For example, the Kobayashi score includes seven variables and has been widely used in Japanese populations ( 11 , 31 ). While these scoring systems show good sensitivity in Asian populations, their performance may vary in other regions ( 2 ). For patients resistant to initial IVIG therapy, second-line treatments are crucial. These may include corticosteroids, infliximab, or cyclosporine. Several studies in our review [e.g., Wu et al. ( 9 ); Cui et al. ( 4 )] mentioned the use of adjunctive treatments, particularly corticosteroids, in refractory cases. According to AHA guidelines, early intensification of therapy in high-risk cases is recommended to reduce coronary complications ( 32 ). The integration of such predictive models into clinical practice could enhance the precision of treatment plans and improve patient outcomes. The pathogenesis of KD and the mechanisms underlying IVIG resistance remain areas of active investigation. Further research into the molecular mechanisms driving IVIG resistance could uncover new therapeutic targets and improve the effectiveness of existing treatments. For instance, studies have suggested that genetic factors may influence an individual's response to IVIG, highlighting the potential for genetic screening in the future ( 33 ). In addition to clinical and molecular research, epidemiological studies are essential to understand the broader impact of IVIG resistance in KD. Variations in resistance prevalence across different populations and regions suggest that environmental and genetic factors may play a role. This meta-analysis provides a global perspective on IVIG resistance, emphasizing the need for international collaboration in KD research. In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis have elucidated the prevalence and significant risk factors associated with IVIG resistance in KD. These findings emphasize the critical need for early identification and personalized treatment approaches to mitigate the risk of severe cardiac complications. Future research should continue to explore the molecular and genetic underpinnings of IVIG resistance, ultimately aiming to enhance therapeutic strategies and improve patient outcomes in KD. Limitations This review is subject to limitations inherent in meta-analyses, including publication bias and variability in study methodologies. Additionally, the heterogeneity among populations studied may affect the generalizability of findings. Conclusion The prevalence of IVIG resistance in Kawasaki disease remains a critical concern, affecting treatment outcomes and long-term cardiovascular health. Future research should focus on refining predictive scoring systems and exploring alternative treatment options for resistant cases. documents.title: Measles vaccine effectiveness in African children: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Measles is an extremely contagious viral disease that can be prevented through vaccination. It is caused by the measles virus and presents with symptoms such as high fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a distinctive rash. Complications may include pneumonia, diarrhoea, and neurological issues. The disease spreads through respiratory droplets and continues to pose a significant public health challenge, especially in Africa, despite vaccination efforts.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to estimate the pooled vaccine effectiveness of measles vaccines among African children, providing insights into immunization program success and informing policy decisions on vaccine distribution and resource allocation.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, search was conducted in databases including PubMed/Medline, Science Direct, HINARI, Cochrane/Wiley library, Europe PMC, and grey literatures like Google Scholar up to March 2024. Cross-sectional studies assessed measles vaccine effectiveness in African children aged nine months and above were included. Data was extracted using JBI extraction tool and entered into microsoft excel and analysed via STATA version 20.1 using random effect model.
RESULTS: From 5295 identified articles, 18 met the inclusion criteria, encompassing 26,470 children from 13 African countries. The pooled measles vaccine effectiveness was 68.58%, with significant heterogeneity (I2 = 99.66%, p < 0.001). Subgroup analysis showed variability in vaccine effectiveness by study period, with higher effectiveness in studies conducted after the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) in 2012.
CONCLUSION: Measles vaccine effectiveness varies in African regions, ranging from 98.4% in Nigeria to 36.5% in Mozambique, with an overall effectiveness of 68.58% and high heterogeneity among studies. Optimizing vaccine distribution, increasing coverage, and prompt administration are important for enhancing effectiveness. Continued support for GVAP strategies and further research is needed to understand factors affecting vaccine performance and improve immunization efforts in Africa.
documents.conclusions: Measles vaccine effectiveness varies in African regions, ranging from 98.4% in Nigeria to 36.5% in Mozambique, with an overall effectiveness of 68.58% and high heterogeneity among studies. Optimizing vaccine distribution, increasing coverage, and prompt administration are important for enhancing effectiveness. Continued support for GVAP strategies and further research is needed to understand factors affecting vaccine performance and improve immunization efforts in Africa.

Introduction Measles is a viral disease caused by the measles virus, which belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family and the Morbillivirus genus. It is an acute respiratory illness that is highly contagious and preventable through vaccination [ 1 ]. Patients infected with measles exhibit symptoms such as high fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis, and a distinctive rash that typically begins on the face and then spreads to the rest of the body [ 2 ]. Those with acute measles are the only source of infection, remaining contagious from the last 1–2 days of the incubation period until five days after the skin rash appears [ 3 ]. Transmission occurs via the respiratory route, through respiratory droplets or aerosolized particles [ 2 ]. In earlier periods, measles was an almost invariably fatal childhood disease, with periodic outbreaks causing widespread morbidity and mortality [ 4 ]. Measles infection can lead to complications affecting many organs. It often results in conditions such as otitis media, laryngotracheobronchitis, pneumonia, stomatitis, diarrhoea, and in severe cases, death [ 1 , 4 ]. Neurological complications, though rare, are serious and can occur during or shortly after the acute disease as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, or months to years later as measles inclusion body encephalitis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis [ 1 ]. Additionally, measles infection can predispose patients to secondary bacterial infections and exacerbate or reactivate tuberculosis due to its impact on the immune system [ 3 , 4 ]. The strategy for measles control and elimination relies heavily on vaccination programs. Routinely, measles vaccination is carried out through the administration of the measles-containing vaccine (MCV) in two doses: the first dose is scheduled for infants between 9 and 12 months of age, and the second dose is given between 15 and 18 months of age or upon school entry. The second dose boosts immunity and serves as a catch-up for those not fully protected by the first dose. Ideally, the first dose provides approximately 85% protection, which can increase to 95% with the second dose. This high level of efficacy is achieved when 95% of the population is vaccinated, ensuring herd immunity and protecting those who cannot be vaccinated, such as infants and individuals with certain medical conditions [ 5 , 6 ]. Since the introduction of the measles vaccine in 1963, there has been a dramatic global reduction in measles incidence and its complications. Vaccination campaigns and the inclusion of the measles vaccine in national immunization programs have significantly decreased the disease’s global burden [ 4 ]. Global efforts, guided by strategies such as the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) 2011–2020 and the Measles & Rubella Initiative (M&RI), aim to achieve and sustain high vaccination coverage, conduct effective surveillance, and provide rapid outbreak response [ 7 ]. These initiatives have led to significant reductions in measles incidence and mortality worldwide, with some regions achieving measles elimination status. Between 2000 and 2018, measles incidence in Africa decreased by 86%, and measles-related deaths decreased by 92% due to increased vaccination coverage and improved outbreak response efforts [ 8 ]. Despite extensive efforts, measles remains endemic in many African countries, with periodic outbreaks posing significant public health concerns. In 2018, Africa accounted for a substantial proportion of global measles cases, with large outbreaks occurring in countries such as Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and Ethiopia [ 9 ]. More recently, measles cases in 2022 increased by 18%, and deaths rose by 43% globally compared to 2021, highlighting the critical nature of this public health problem [ 10 ]. The occurrence of measles outbreaks in many African countries highlights immunity gaps and necessitates further investigation into the measles vaccine’s effectiveness in real-world settings. Various factors can influence vaccine effectiveness, including nutritional status [ 11 ], vaccine storage and handling [ 12 ], administration [ 5 ], hesitancy [ 13 ], waning immunity [ 6 ], genetic variation of the measles virus [ 14 , 15 ], immune suppression [ 16 , 17 ], interference from maternal antibodies [ 16 , 18 ], sub-optimal vaccine coverage [ 19 ], vaccine failure [ 20 ], and timing [ 16 , 21 ]. To our knowledge, there has not been a meta-analysis study showing a single pooled estimate of vaccine effectiveness levels among vaccinated African children. Thus, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesize available evidence, providing valuable insights about the degree of success regarding immunization programs and offering an estimate of the pooled vaccine effectiveness level for policy-makers to make informed decisions about vaccine distribution, prioritize vulnerable populations, and allocate resources efficiently in the African context. Moreover, the measles prevention and control strategy aligned with the GVAP globally. In this context, the anticipated impact of the GVAP in Africa is expected to enhance measles prevention and control efforts. However, the effectiveness of the measles vaccine pre- and post-GVAP endorsement remains unexplored. To assess the significance of the GVAP endorsement, it is imperative to consider the level of measles vaccine effectiveness prior to the GVAP era compared to the post-GVAP period. Methods Registration and protocol This review protocol is registered with the National Institute for Health Research’s PROSPERO, the international prospective register of systematic reviews, under registration number CRD42024570494. Detailed information can be found at https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/#recordDetails . Searching strategy This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, version 2022, to search the scientific literature (Supplementary 1). We initially searched for published articles in PubMed/Medline, ScienceDirect, HINARI, the Cochrane/Wiley Library, Europe PMC, and Google Scholar, without any restrictions on the year of publication. The search used the following keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH): “Children in Africa,” “Vaccine,” “Measles,” “Rubeola,” “Africa,” “Child (MeSH),” “Measles Vaccine (MeSH),” and “Measles (MeSH),” either separately or in combination using the Boolean operators “OR” and “AND.”. The search for articles was conducted over nearly two months, from February 10, 2024, to March 5, 2024. The literature search was finalized and updated on March 5, 2024. All published articles up to March 5, 2024 were retrieved and evaluated for eligibility and inclusion in this review. Solely peer-reviewed original articles published in English were taken into consideration. Moreover, we scrutinized the bibliographies of all identified articles to discover additional pertinent studies and references. Population Infants vaccinated at 9 months of age and beyond with the measles vaccine. Intervention Administration of the measles vaccine. Comparator None. Outcome The objective of this systematic review was to determine the proportion of measles-vaccinated children in Africa who were shielded from measles infection. Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria Articles with a cross-sectional study design that reported the measles incidence and level of measles vaccine effectiveness in children younger than five years in Africa were considered for analysis. Articles published in non-English language were also included in the analysis after translation to English language with google translate. The translation was conducted through a systematic approach, involving translations paragraph by paragraph ensuring the accuracy and integrity of the information. Exclusion criteria In conducting our analysis, we only considered original research articles and studies with both abstracts and full documents available. We also excluded any studies conducted using a “high”-titer (5.0 log 10 pfu/dose), as well as review papers, conference papers, randomized control trials, and case control studies. Definition of terms Vaccine effectiveness : measures how well a vaccine performs in the real world, typically expressed as a percentage reduction in disease among vaccinated individuals compared to unvaccinated individuals which is a different concept from vaccine efficacy. A vaccine’s efficacy is measured in a controlled clinical trial and is based on how many people who got vaccinated developed the ‘outcome of interest’ (usually disease) compared with how many people who got the placebo (dummy vaccine) developed the same outcome [ 22 ]. The measles vaccine effectiveness in the included articles were calculated using the formula: VE=((PPV − PCV)/PPV)×100. where PPV is the proportion of population vaccinated, and PCV is the proportion of cases in vaccinated. Study selection and screening All articles identified through our search strategy exported to End Note 20.1 and duplicates were removed. Based on their titles and abstract, two independent researchers screened the identified articles. In cases of disagreement, discussions were took place between the researchers during the screening and selection process. If a consensus could not be reached after discussions, a third researcher was consulted to facilitate resolution. Duplicate article identification and screening process was performed through End Note 20.1. Articles deemed eligible after screening were included for further examination. Prior to data collection, the chosen articles were retrieved and reviewed to assess their appropriateness [ 23 ]. The search methodology was visually represented in a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flowchart illustrating the studies that were either included or excluded, along with the reasons for exclusion (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram for screening and selection process of articles for measles vaccine effectiveness systematic review among vaccinated children in Africa Quality assessment We employed critical appraisal tools to evaluate the quality of prevalence studies included in JBI systematic reviews [ 24 ]. This process involved two researchers who independently evaluated the quality of the included studies. Each researcher carefully analysed the methodology, data analysis, and overall robustness of the studies to ensure a comprehensive evaluation. In order to determine the quality score of the articles, we calculated the average quality assessment score from the two researchers and utilized to ascertain the quality score of the articles (Supporting Information: S1). Data extraction process Data extraction was conducted through Joanna Briggs Institute data extraction tool updated in 2024 [ 24 ] following a thorough review of abstracts and full texts carried out by two independent researchers. Data extraction tool used the Microsoft excel sheet through which data elements were captured. The excel extracted data includes the author’s name, publication year, country, study design, sample size, age, vaccine type, study data type, and vaccine effectiveness level. The researchers determined the data elements, African sub-region and study period based on the global vaccine action plan for elimination plan from the country where the study conducted and year of study respectively. Data analysis The Excel-extracted data was subsequently imported into statistical software for data analysis (STATA) version 20.1 and utilized for conducting the meta-analysis. Vaccine effectiveness was determined using a random effects model with a 95% confidence interval (CI). A Forest plot was utilized to determine the magnitude of protection provided to vaccinated children with a 95% CI. Subgroup analysis was conducted to address any potential heterogeneity present. Heterogeneity and publication bias Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic. If the I 2 statistic falls below 25%, between 25 and 50%, or exceeds 50%, the level of heterogeneity was categorized as low, moderate, or high respectively [ 24 ]. A sensitivity analysis was conducted by systematically excluding one study at a time to ensure that no single study unduly influenced the results. Statistical significance was defined as a p-value below 0.05. Examination for publication bias was carried out utilizing Egger’s regression test, with graphical representation through a standard funnel plot for studies numbering ten or more. A p-value below 0.10 in Egger’s test was deemed to indicate significant bias. Results Study characteristics Initially, we identified 5295 articles from different databases. After removal of seven duplicate articles, we identified 5264 unique articles. The identified articles were screened through their titles and abstract. Based on the title and abstract screening, 52,456 articles were excluded from analysis. Nineteen articles were assessed for eligibility and seven articles were excluded from analysis. Finally, 18 articles were included in this review after conducting a rigorous screening process. All articles were a cross sectional studies conducted in 13 African countries. We identified seven articles in the Eastern Africa, Five articles in the western, four articles in the central, one articles in the South, one article in the North sub-regions of Africa. In the review, the overall sample size pooled from all articles was 26,470 children aged nine months and above with a minimum of 143 study participants in Cameroon and a maximum of study participants of 8127 from South Africa. Of the total 18 articles, 11 articles were published before the period of global vaccine action plan (GVAP) held on 2012 to eliminate measles by the year. Vaccine effectiveness across country This comprehensive systematic analysis integrated individual studies from most African countries, with the exception of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Ethiopia, Gambia, and Mozambique where multiple articles were accessed and included in the analysis. Measles vaccine effectiveness demonstrates variability across diverse regions and nations within the continent of Africa. The highest reported measles vaccine effectiveness was 98.4% in Nigeria, while the lowest was 36.5% in Mozambique. Additionally, the measles vaccine effectiveness was reported as follows: 89.19% in Gambia, 84.1% in Kenya, 80.7% in Egypt, 68% in Guinea-Bissau, 67.8% in Guinea, and 74% in Uganda. In countries where more than two articles were accessed, Ethiopia showed vaccine effectiveness of 71.95% and 75.3%. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, effectiveness was 53.9% in semi-urban areas and 78.7% in rural areas. In Mozambique, effectiveness was 40% in 1985, 36.5% in 1986 in the rural village of Nampula, and 59% in the rural village of Beira. Vaccine effectiveness across African sub-region More than two articles were identified in the Western, Eastern, and Central regions of Africa, while only single studies were accessed from the Southern and Northern African sub-regions. The analysis showed a higher level of measles vaccine effectiveness in the West African sub-region, ranging from 67.8% in Guinea to 89.5% in Gambia and 98.4% in Nigeria. In the Eastern part of Africa, the measles vaccine effectiveness ranged from 36.5% in Mozambique to 84.1% in Kenya. Similarly, in the Central African region, the measles vaccine effectiveness ranged from 40% in Cameroon and Chad to 78.7% in the rural areas of the Democratic Republic of Congo. Moreover, a single reports from the Northern and Southern sub-regions of Africa showed measles vaccine effectiveness of 80.7% in Egypt and 80% in South Africa (Table 1 ). The pooled effect size or vaccine effectiveness was 68.58% (95% CI:59.99–77.16) with a heterogeneity index ( I 2 ) of 99.66% ( p < 0.001) (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Forest plot of the measles vaccine effectiveness among vaccinated children in Africa Sub-group analysis To address the significant level of heterogeneity, a subgroup analysis was performed by using the period of the study conducted on vaccine effectiveness before and after the Global Vaccine Action Plan in 2012. We have accessed eight articles after and eleven articles before the period of GVAP. This analysis revealed that the pooled vaccine effectiveness was higher in studies conducted after the Global Vaccine Action Plan at 79.55 (70.16–88.94) compared to studies conducted before the plan at 61.54 (50.67–72.41), with heterogeneity indices of 99.53% and 99.66% respectively (Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Forest plot showing measles vaccine effectiveness by period of study before and after the global vaccine action plan of 2012 for measles elimination by 2020 among vaccinated children in African Heterogeneity and publication bias The overall heterogeneity of this systematic review and meta-analysis was I 2 = 99.66% ( p < 0.001), indicating a significant heterogeneity among the studies included. To address and comprehend the root cause of this diversity, we undertook a subgroup analysis based on the study period outlined in the global vaccine action plan of 2012, aiming for measles elimination by 2020. Nonetheless, due to the unavailability of multiple articles by country and sub-region, conducting a subgroup analysis by country and sub-region was not feasible. Egger test for detecting small-study effects was executed to assess the presence of publication bias, while a funnel plot was generated to visually represent this bias. Upon visual examination of the funnel plot, an asymmetric distribution of studies was observed, which was statistically significant, as indicated by the Egger test ( p = 0.008), thereby confirming the existence of publication bias (Fig. 4 ). Fig. 4 Funnel plot showing publication bias regarding measles vaccine effectiveness among vaccinated children in Africa Discussion The current systematic review and meta-analysis was undertaken to determine the pooled level of protection provided by the measles vaccine in studies involving African children. The pooled measles vaccine effectiveness level in this review (68.58%) to prevent measles infection of African children is suboptimal. It seems that it requires more actions to attain WHO goal of measles elimination by attaining a 90% and 95% protection through vaccination with one dose and two doses respectively. This pooled vaccine effectiveness level in African children in our review is by far low compared with the vaccine effectiveness level reported from measles vaccine effectiveness assessment report of Australia national surveillance data, 96.7% [ 41 ] and case control study in Dhaka, Bangladesh 80% [ 42 ], Bosnia and Herzegovina measles outbreak assessment, 91.9 for single dose and 97.3% for two dose [ 43 ], Romania measles epidemic analysis, 89% for one dose and 96% for two dose [ 44 ]. This could be explained with the variation in the infrastructures used for measles vaccine storage, transport and handling. In most African countries, the infrastructures used in the proper management of vaccines including vaccine storage, transport and handling facilities are scares [ 45 ] In addition, the low measles vaccine effectiveness level in African continent could be related with the variation in the standard of health care system in that the standard of health care provision in developed world assisted with well equipped infrastructure and skilled manpower. The well equipped infrastructures would help to increase the access of vaccination services to all susceptible and high risk groups, populations or areas. Low levels of measles vaccine effectiveness in the African region expose many African children to measles infections, leading to numerous outbreaks and ongoing transmissions throughout the continent. This phenomenon is closely linked to the high prevalence of measles epidemiology and the frequent occurrence of outbreaks in various African countries. Additionally, it serves as a clear indication that the African region is falling behind in implementing crucial measles prevention and control measures outlined in the global vaccine action plan of 2012. Addressing the suboptimal measles vaccine effectiveness level requires immediate action to enhance vaccine coverage, particularly in hard-to-reach areas within each African country. In this review, it is noted that the highest level of vaccine effectiveness was observed in Nigeria, 98.4% and lowest was observed in Mozambique, 36.5% and Cameron, 40%. This could be related to the variation in the years of study in that the health care system during earlier study periods different from the current health care system. For instance, the vaccine effectiveness study conducted in Cameron, and Mozambique were in 1976 and 1990 which are long years back from now indicating the variation in the health care system with improved health care system during the current periods. Moreover, the high effectiveness of the measles vaccine in Nigeria may be associated with the country’s socio-economic standing, given that Nigeria possesses a relatively favourable socio-economic status. Besides, a higher level of vaccine effectiveness was observed in countries within West African and North African sub-regions and lower level of vaccine effectiveness in Central Africa sub-region and Easter African sub-regions comparatively. This might be associated with the variation in the socio-economic status and the health care system among the countries within the sub regions enrolled in this review. Additionally, it may be correlated with the disparity in the duration of research among the included studies, as most of the studies in the Northern and Western sub-regions of Africa in this analysis were conducted in more recent periods following the endorsement of measles prevention and control initiatives, in contrast to those carried out in the Eastern and Central African countries. A sub-group analysis conducted to compare results before and after the implementation of the Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) in 2012 unveiled a marginal increase in the pooled effectiveness of measles vaccines in studies conducted post-GVAP 2012 endorsement. This slight enhancement in measles vaccine effectiveness subsequent to the GVAP endorsement is likely attributable to the interventions introduced by the plan. The GVAP was endorsed with the aim of ensuring global attainment of vaccine coverage targets, irrespective of geographical location, and to facilitate fair vaccine accessibility to all demographics for all vaccine-preventable diseases. This plan advocates for the advancement and implementation of novel and under-utilized vaccines while integrating immunization programs with other healthcare services to maximize their impact [ 46 ]. The effectiveness of the measles vaccine in this analysis during the pre-Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) era in Africa is comparatively lower than that of developed nations in the same period, as evidenced by studies conducted in the United Kingdom [ 47 ], showing 88% effectiveness for one dose and 95% for two doses, and in Pakistan [ 48 ] showing 83% effectiveness. Similarly, a reduced level of measles vaccine effectiveness was also observed in African countries during the post-Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) era. For example, Germany [ 49 ] exhibited a high level of measles vaccine effectiveness level ranging from 90 to 97% during post-Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP) periods. This disparity can be attributed to the impact of insufficient measles vaccine coverage in many low-income African nations, influenced by factors such as conflict, displacement, educational levels, socio-economic status, limited access to healthcare, and fragile healthcare systems [ 50 ]. Furthermore, the diminished effectiveness of the measles vaccine in the African context may be associated with nutritional deficiencies, the burden of other infectious diseases, and pool of immuno-compromised populations, such that the high prevalence of HIV, nutritional deficiencies and other infectious disease are more pronounced in African countries [ 51 ]. This trend continues to impact numerous African nations, resulting in frequent measles outbreaks that lead to a high incidence of morbidity and mortality among children. The overall pooled measles vaccine effectiveness in this study is influenced by a notable degree of heterogeneity. This heterogeneity may stem from the diversity in demographics, encompassing factors like age, geographical location, socio-economic status, and health conditions of the study cohorts [ 52 ], discrepancies across healthcare systems and immunization protocols [ 53 , 54 ], variations in the timing and quantity of vaccine doses administered [ 52 ], as well as the variability in how outcomes are defined and reported such as distinguishing between laboratory-confirmed cases and clinically diagnosed cases all contribute to this heterogeneity. Strength and limitation Despite the comprehensive nature of this systematic review and meta-analysis, which includes evidence from a wide range of publication years and languages on measles vaccine effectiveness, some limitations remain that future research should address. Notably, the review only included articles primarily relied on cross-sectional studies, which are known to have relatively lower evidential power compared to other study designs. Moreover, presence of high statistical heterogeneity and publication bias among the included studies would decrease the generalization of evidence from this review. Some studies included in the analysis date back several years, which may not accurately reflect current vaccine effectiveness due to changes in vaccination practices, healthcare infrastructure, and disease epidemiology. For instance, studies from the 1970s and 1990s may not be representative of today’s healthcare contexts. Conclusion In conclusion, a review of 18 studies from thirteen African countries shows measles vaccine effectiveness at 68.58%. Nigeria had the highest effectiveness (98.4%) and Mozambique the lowest (36.5%). West Africa had better effectiveness than Central Africa. Studies post GVAP 2012 plan had higher effectiveness (79.55%) than pre-plan studies (61.54%). Targeted interventions are crucial in low effectiveness areas. Customized strategies are needed, including reinforcing routine immunization and special campaigns. Improving vaccine access in remote areas is vital. Support for GVAP strategies is key for increased coverage and effectiveness. Future research should explore diverse study designs and collaborate with local researchers to understand challenges and socio-economic impacts. Developing new vaccines for measles prevention is recommended. Electronic supplementary material Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material. documents.title: The prevalence of Trichomonas vaginalis infection among the female population of Iran: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract: Trichomonas vaginalis is a protozoan parasite and probably one of the main causes of adverse birth outcomes. Still, there is a paucity of information regarding the burden of T. vaginalis infection in Iranian women. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on trichomoniasis among females in Iran from January 2000 to January 2023. We searched multiple electronic databases (PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, ProQuest, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Scientific Information Database, Iran Medex, Magiran and Iran Doc) and identified 108 articles with a total of 200 728 women. Using a random effects model, we found a pooled prevalence of 4.30% (95% CI 3.23 to 5.52%). Subgroup analysis, also, demonstrated a statistically significant association between the T. vaginalis prevalence in Iranian women, and the age range, city, sample type, being in prison, sex working and symptomatic infections. Our findings provide important information for healthcare authorities and can inform prevention strategies against trichomoniasis in Iran.

Introduction Trichomoniasis, caused by the flagellated anaerobe Trichomonas vaginalis (TV), is a prevalent sexually transmissible infection (STI) with approximately 156 million new cases annually among both men and women globally. 1 In resource-limited settings, TV infection has been found to be more prevalent than some bacterial STIs, such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae . 2 A number of risk factors have been recognized as being associated with the increased risk of trichomoniasis, comprising poor urogenital hygiene, high-risk sexual practices and bacterial vaginosis. 3 Humans are the only natural hosts of TV, and the organism can be found through urogenital tracts, including the vagina, uterus and cervix in women, as well as the urethra and prostate gland in men. 4 The infection is primarily asymptomatic in both men and women; hence, they may spread it unwittingly to their partners. The majority of women manifest symptoms such as vulvar irritation and inflammation, frothy vaginal discharge and dyspareunia. 5 , 6 Of note, the so-called pathognomonic ‘strawberry cervix’ is a rare sign due to the spot bleeding in cervical mucosa. 7 Trichomoniasis burden in women of childbearing age significantly impacts the pregnancy outcomes. Based on a recent meta-analysis on adverse birth outcomes, TV infection may substantially increase the possibility of preterm delivery (PTD), prelabor rupture of membranes and low birth weight (LBW) by 1.27% (95% CI 1.08 to 1.5%), 1.87% (95% CI 1.53 to 2.29%) and 2.12% (95% CI 1.15 to 3.91%), respectively. 8 Also, literature exists on the association between TV and pelvic inflammatory disease 9 and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. 10 Meanwhile, TV is an important contributing factor in the acquisition of HIV infection by about 1.5% (95% CI 1.3 to 1.7%). 11 According to various clinical sequelae of TV infection, multiple studies have focused on this common protozoan parasite, particularly in underdeveloped countries. In Iran, a large Middle Eastern country, several investigations have reported the prevalence rate of TV among different groups of women. 4 Previously, in 2015, Hezarjaribi et al. performed a limited systematic review and meta-analysis on this issue, although they missed considering the likely subgroups as potential risk factors of TV infection in Iran. 12 Thus, we designed and conducted the current comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis to provide updated details regarding the prevalence of TV infection among the female population of Iran and to detect potential risk factors. Methods The present systematic review and meta-analysis follows the Preferred Reporting Items in Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guideline to ensure accurate and transparent reporting. 13 Search strategy To evaluate the epidemiological status of TV infection among different groups of Iranian women, we designed a systematic review based on screening the literature released online in both the English and Persian languages. Six English databases (PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, ProQuest, Web of Science and Google Scholar) and four Persian databases (Scientific Information Database, Iran Medex, Magiran and Iran Doc) were searched for published papers from January 2000 to January 2023. The current review was performed using medical subject headings (MeSH) terms, including ‘ Trichomonas vaginalis ’, ‘ T. vaginalis ’, ‘Trichomoniasis’, ‘Prevalence’, ‘Epidemiology’, ‘Iran’, ‘Islamic Republic of Iran’, ‘Women’ and ‘Girls’, alone or in combination, to identify eligible studies on TV infection among Iranian women. Study selection and data extraction Based on inclusion criteria, cross-sectional studies based on assessing TV infection in Iranian women using parasitological (microscopy, culture) and molecular techniques were included. To assess eligibility, all papers were reviewed by two independent reviewers. Review articles, letters to the editor and studies without an accurate sample size and positive number of TV cases were excluded from this review. Those selected were read carefully, and contradictions among studies were resolved by discussion and consensus. Next, the desired data were collected precisely using a data extraction form, including the first author, publication year, city, sample size, positive cases, sample type, diagnostic method, age range, residential area, symptomatic/asymptomatic infection, pregnancy, abortion, prisoner and sex worker. Meta-analysis The prevalence and its 95% CI of TV infection among Iranian women were estimated for individual studies. A forest plot was used to present the results of the meta-analysis, exhibited as estimates of prevalence and their 95% CIs for each study with the summary measure. Furthermore, forest plot analysis was provided for each included subgroup. Heterogeneity and inconsistency were evaluated using Cochran's Q and I 2 statistics, respectively. Furthermore, a funnel plot based on Egger's regression test was designed to assess small study effects and publication bias. According to the results of the heterogeneity test, either Der Simonian and Laird's random-effects method or Mantel–Haenszel's fixed-effects method was used to pool the estimations. Quality assessment The included studies were evaluated for quality using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale ( Supplementary Table 1 ). 14 Three factors made up the scoring system: selection (a maximum of five stars), comparability (a maximum of two stars) and result (a maximum of three stars). Results After searching multiple databases, a total of 1092 papers were identified, from which 577 papers were screened after removing duplicates and 398 papers were excluded based on the inclusion criteria. The eligibility assessment was conducted on 179 full-text articles and 10 studies were excluded because of insufficient data. Of the remaining studies, six had overlapping data, six lacked participant information and 49 papers contained no original data. A total of 108 articles containing 164 datasets were included in the meta-analysis based on the critical appraisal criteria (Figure 1 and Table 1 ). Figure 1. The boxes indicate the effect size of the studies (prevalence) and the whiskers indicate its CI for corresponding effect size. Based on the included studies, a map was created using QGIS3 software ( https://qgis.org/en/site/ ) to demonstrate the prevalence of trichomoniasis among the female population of Iran in different geographical regions (Figure 3 ). Figure 3. The prevalence of trichomoniasis among the female population of Iran in different geographical regions based on the included studies ( https://qgis.org/en/site/ ). Subgroup analysis was also performed to determine the weighted prevalence in comparison with 11 different parameters, namely, mean age, residential status, city, sample type, diagnostic method, symptomatic or asymptomatic infection, being a prisoner, being a sex worker, pregnancy status, abortion, and using condoms or other devices. Regarding cities, most investigations were performed among women in Tehran and Hamadan, with 16 (4.34% [95% CI 1.96 to 7.54%]) and 7 (2.28% [95% CI 0.78 to 4.43%]) records, respectively; nevertheless, the highest prevalence rates were found in Rafsanjan (only one study), Qom (three studies) and Khorramabad (a single study), with 56.17% (95% CI 48.48 to 63.58%), 20.22% (95% CI 10 to 32.9%) and 18.75% (95% CI 13.46 to 25.5%), respectively. Of note, the lowest prevalences were reported from Sanandaj (0.0% [95% CI 0.0 to 1.73%]), Shahrood (0.33% [95% CI 0.06 to 1.86%]) and Bahar (0.47% [95% CI 0.18 to 1.2%]). The prevalence was shown to decrease with increasing age range, so that the highest and lowest frequency of TV infection were estimated in the 25–30 y (5.07% [95% CI 2.27 to 8.84%]) and >35 y (2.29% [95% CI 0.21 to 6.28%]) age groups, respectively. Interestingly, the prevalence rate was higher in urban settings (2.43% [95% CI 1.55 to 3.49%]) than in rural areas (1.42% [95% CI 0.3 to 3.14%]). Considerably higher prevalence of TV infection was reported in vaginal swab samples (4.29% [95% CI 3.21 to 5.51%]) than in urine specimens (1.84% [95% CI 0.79 to 3.29%]). Based on diagnostic methods, the highest prevalence rate was detected using the PCR technique with 8.88% (95% CI 3.48 to 16.37%), followed by the culture method (3.93% [95% CI 2.66 to 5.42%]) and microscopy (3.49% [95% CI 2.59 to 4.52%]). In 19 studies, symptomatic infection was evaluated, leading to a prevalence of 13.27% (95% CI 8.66 to 18.65%) of TV infection, whereas a prevalence of 4.22% (95% CI 1.65 to 7.81%) was documented for asymptomatic infections (eight studies). In addition, the prevalence of TV infection was estimated to be higher in those women with pregnancy (4.44% [95% CI 0.79 to 10.61%]), having a history of abortion (15.27% [95% CI 0.06 to 46.46%]), being a prisoner (18.12% [95% CI 9.55 to 28.63%]) or being a sex worker (2.51% [95% CI 0.00 to 15.59%]), as well as those utilizing condoms and/or other disease-preventing devices (2.44% [95% CI 0.58 to 5.42%]). There was a statistically significant association between TV infection and city (p<0.001), sample type (p=0.005), being a prisoner or sex worker (p<0.001) and symptomatic/asymptomatic infections (p=0.002) (Table 2 and Supplementary Figures 1–4 ).
